questions.question: At what object size does the .NET GC place an allocation on the Large Object Heap (LOH) instead of the normal small-object heap?

choices.text: 85,000 bytes
8,000 bytes
1 MB, matching the default gen 2 segment size
There's no fixed threshold; it depends on available memory

questions.explanation: An object >= 85,000 bytes is allocated on the LOH; this threshold was determined by performance tuning and is a fixed constant, not memory-dependent. 8,000 bytes and 1 MB are plausible-sounding but wrong numbers; 'depends on memory' misdescribes it as dynamic when it's a fixed threshold.

questions.question: Why is boxing a value type considered expensive?

choices.text: It requires a network round trip to the CLR type registry
It allocates a new object on the managed heap and adds GC pressure
It permanently locks the value type's memory for the process lifetime
It converts the value to a string internally before storing it

questions.explanation: Boxing allocates a heap object and copies the value into it, adding GC pressure and defeating the point of using a value type. There's no network call, no permanent lock, and no implicit string conversion involved.

questions.question: When an `await` is reached and the awaited task is already completed, what happens?

choices.text: The state machine always allocates on the heap and schedules a continuation
The method restarts execution from the beginning
Execution continues synchronously inline, with no thread yield
The thread pool spins up a new thread to finish the method

questions.explanation: If the awaiter's IsCompleted is already true, MoveNext() just continues executing inline — no continuation registration, no thread yield, and (if the whole method completes this way) potentially no heap allocation at all for the state machine. It doesn't restart the method or spin up a new thread.

questions.question: What effect does `ConfigureAwait(false)` have inside an ASP.NET Core request-handling method?

choices.text: It eliminates thread-pool starvation risk under any load
It forces the continuation back onto the original request thread
It suppresses exception propagation from the awaited task
ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, so it's a no-op here

questions.explanation: ASP.NET Core doesn't install a SynchronizationContext (unlike classic ASP.NET), so continuations already run on arbitrary thread pool threads regardless of ConfigureAwait — it's harmless but provides no benefit there. It doesn't prevent starvation on its own, doesn't force a specific thread, and doesn't touch exception propagation.

questions.question: Why can't a `try/catch` around the call site of a fire-and-forget `async void` method reliably catch its exceptions?

choices.text: It's rethrown on the active thread/context instead of the Task
async void methods aren't permitted to throw exceptions
The CLR automatically swallows exceptions thrown from async void
try/catch can't wrap any method containing an await expression

questions.explanation: There's no Task for async void, so its exceptions can't be stored/observed like a normal async Task method's — they're thrown directly wherever the continuation resumes, bypassing a try/catch at the call site (often crashing the process). They aren't disallowed, aren't silently swallowed, and try/catch works fine around awaited async Task methods.

questions.question: What two conditions together cause the classic async/await deadlock when calling `.Result` or `.Wait()`?

choices.text: Using ValueTask instead of Task causes the deadlock
Running the application in a Debug build configuration
Calling an async method from within a static constructor
A single-threaded context and a synchronous block

questions.explanation: The deadlock needs a context (UI thread, classic ASP.NET request thread) that the continuation is captured to and blocked on — the blocked thread can never run the continuation, so the awaited task never completes. ValueTask, Debug builds, and static constructors aren't the cause.

questions.question: Which GC mode is the ASP.NET Core default, and why?

choices.text: Workstation GC, because it minimizes memory footprint for containers
Only concurrent GC is used, with generational collection disabled entirely
Server GC, since spare cores favor parallel throughput-oriented collection
There is no default GC mode; it must always be explicitly configured

questions.explanation: Server GC runs a dedicated heap and GC thread per logical core in parallel, trading memory for throughput — the right trade-off for a typical server with spare cores, which is why it's the ASP.NET Core default. Workstation GC is the better fit for memory-constrained, low-CPU scenarios (e.g., many 1-core containers), not the ASP.NET Core default; the runtime does have a default even if unconfigured.

questions.question: What is unsafe about awaiting the same `ValueTask` (or `ValueTask<T>`) more than once?

choices.text: The pooled backing source resets, making a second await unsafe
Nothing — ValueTask can be awaited multiple times just like Task
The compiler rejects a second await with a compile-time error
It always deadlocks the thread that awaits it a second time

questions.explanation: Unlike Task (a plain object safe to observe multiple times), a ValueTask may back onto a pooled IValueTaskSource that gets reset once consumed — awaiting it again can throw, return stale data, or corrupt an unrelated operation reusing the same pooled object. It's not compile-time checked and doesn't inherently deadlock.

questions.question: You inject a Scoped service directly into a Singleton in ASP.NET Core's DI container. What's the correct description of the risk and the built-in safety net?

choices.text: The container always throws at startup, in every environment — this can never ship
It works correctly and is the recommended way to consume scoped services from singletons
The container silently creates a fresh scope automatically for each call
It becomes a captive dependency; validation only throws by default in Development

questions.explanation: This is a captive dependency: the singleton holds the scoped instance for its entire lifetime instead of getting a fresh one per request. Microsoft's docs note that scope-validation throwing this error by default only happens in the Development environment (not always, and not in every environment) — so it can slip through unnoticed in other environments. It's not automatically safe, and DI does not auto-create a new scope per call for you.

questions.question: What's the standard EF Core fix for the N+1 query problem caused by lazily-loaded navigation properties accessed in a loop?

choices.text: Wrap the loop in a single database transaction
Disable the database's query result cache
Use eager loading via .Include()/.ThenInclude() for one JOIN query
Switch the DbContext lifetime from Scoped to Singleton
Increase the database connection pool size limit

questions.explanation: .Include()/.ThenInclude() (or explicit .Load() calls) fetch related data as part of the initial query via a JOIN, turning N+1 round trips into one (or a controlled few). A transaction, connection pool size, and query caching don't address the root cause of issuing one query per entity; making DbContext a Singleton is actively wrong and unsafe (DbContext is not thread-safe and is meant to be Scoped).
